Judgment on Jerusalem's confident rulers (verses 1–13)

When Satan cannot persuade people that God's judgment is uncertain, he tries to make them believe it is far away.

The rulers of Jerusalem imagined themselves safe inside their city.

They compared its walls to a cooking pot and themselves to the meat protected inside.

They expected the walls to withstand the siege as confidently as a pot withstands the heat beneath it.

But people who flatter themselves toward destruction must be warned that they will have no peace while continuing in sin.

Those who would remain in the city were not the secure living inhabitants but the people buried there.

Those who feel most secure may be the least safe.

God may single out a particular sinner's judgment to warn others.

Yet Henry does not claim certainty about exactly when Pelatiah died—whether during the vision's events or near their future fulfillment.

Like Ezekiel, we should be deeply moved by the sudden death of others and continue pleading for God's mercy toward those who remain.

God promises to give his people new hearts (verses 14–21)

The godly Israelites in Babylon were scorned by those still living in Jerusalem.

But God gave the exiles gracious promises.

He would give them one heart: a heart firmly devoted to him rather than divided and wavering.

Those who are made holy receive a new spirit—a renewed character and new inclinations.

They act from new principles, follow new rules and seek new goals.

A new name or a new appearance is not enough without a new spirit.

Anyone who is in Christ is a new creation.

A sinful heart is like stone: it does not feel what it should.

People may live amid death and suffering without being concerned or humbled.

The Lord promises to make their hearts tender and responsive.

This is God's own work, a gift he promised.

The change from death to life is wonderful and blessed.

People whose inward principles are renewed will also show changed conduct.

The two belong together.

When sinners recognize how much they need these blessings, let them turn God's promises into prayers offered in Christ's name.

He will fulfill what he has promised.

God's glory withdraws from Jerusalem (verses 22–25)

The vision shows God's presence leaving the city and temple.

It rises from the Mount of Olives, which Henry takes as a picture of Christ's ascension to heaven from that same mountain.

The Lord will never finally abandon his people.

Yet a particular part of the visible church may lose the experience of his presence because of its sins.

Woe to those from whom he withdraws his presence, glory and protection.

Chapter 11
Divine judgments against the wicked at Jerusalem. ( [Ezek.11.1-Ezek.11.13] Ezek 11:1-13) Divine favour towards those in captivity. ( [Ezek.11.14-Ezek.11.21] Ezek 11:14-21) The Divine presence forsakes the city. ( [Ezek.11.22-Ezek.11.25] Ezek 11:22-25)
Verses 1-13 Where Satan cannot persuade men to look upon the judgment to come as uncertain, he gains his point by persuading them to look upon it as at a distance. These wretched rulers dare to say, We are as safe in this city as flesh in a boiling pot; the walls of the city shall be to us as walls of brass, we shall receive no more damage from the besiegers than the caldron does from the fire. When sinners flatter themselves to their own ruin, it is time to tell them they shall have no peace if they go on. None shall remain in possession of the city but those who are buried in it. Those are least safe who are most secure. God is often pleased to single out some sinners for warning to others. Whether Pelatiah died at that time in Jerusalem, or when the fulfilment of the prophecy drew near, is uncertain. Like Ezekiel, we ought to be much affected with the sudden death of others, and we should still plead with the Lord to have mercy on those who remain.
[Ezek.11.14-Ezek.11.21]
Verses 14-21 The pious captives in Babylon were insulted by the Jews who continued in Jerusalem; but God made gracious promises to them. It is promised, that God will give them one heart; a heart firmly fixed for God, and not wavering. All who are made holy have a new spirit, a new temper and dispositions; they act from new principles, walk by new rules, and aim at new ends. A new name, or a new face, will not serve without a new spirit. If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature. The carnal heart, like a stone, cannot be made to feel. Men live among the dead and dying, and are neither concerned nor humbled. He will make their hearts tender and fit to receive impressions: this is God's work, it is his gift by promise; and a wonderful and happy change is wrought by it, from death to life. Their practices shall be agreeable to those principles. These two must and will go together. When the sinner feels his need of these blessings, let him present the promises as prayers in the name of Christ, they will be performed.
[Ezek.11.22-Ezek.11.25]
Verses 22-25 Here is the departure of God's presence from the city and temple. It was from the Mount of Olives that the vision went up, typifying the ascension of Christ to heaven from that very mountain. Though the Lord will not forsake his people, yet he may be driven away from any part of his visible church by their sins, and woe will be upon them when He withdraws his presence, glory, and protection.

Ezekiel pictures the coming exile (verses 1–16)

Ezekiel prepared belongings for departure and broke through the wall of his house at evening, as someone trying to escape an enemy might do.

These actions pictured Zedekiah's behavior and fate.

When God delivers us from trouble, we must give him glory and help others learn from what happened, including by acknowledging our sins.

People brought through suffering to recognize the Lord may themselves become a means through which others come to know him.

The prophet eats and drinks in fear (verses 17–20)

Ezekiel was to eat and drink with fear, anxiety and trembling.

This pictured what the inhabitants of Jerusalem would experience during the siege.

Ministers announcing judgment upon sinners should speak as people who know the terror of the Lord.

Although afflictions may be deeply painful to our bodies and emotions, they can become blessed if they increase our knowledge of God.

Scoffers cannot postpone God's word (verses 21–28)

The Jews took God's patience—which should have led them to repent—as a reason to become more stubborn in sin.

Calling something a common saying does not excuse using it to speak wrongly.

Only a short step separates us from eternity and judgment.

We should therefore prepare for the life to come.

No one can avert the day of judgment by dismissing its warnings or imagining it is far off.

The only safe response is to seek peace with the Lord.

No one will be able to put from himself the evil day, unless by seeking peace with the Lord.

False prophets speak their own inventions (verses 1–9)

When God appoints someone to a task, he also gives wisdom for it.

The false prophets did not speak what they had received from God.

By contrast, the ministers of Christ must proclaim what God has revealed.

These false prophets did not pray or maintain fellowship with heaven.

They devised words designed to please people rather than to do them good.

They did not resist sin or call people to repentance.

Instead, they flattered people into empty expectations.

Such teachers widen the breach between sinners and God.

They persuade people they are entitled to eternal life while God's wrath still rests upon them.

Whitewashed walls cannot stand (verses 10–16)

One false prophet built the wall by announcing that Jerusalem would succeed and escape danger.

That promise made him popular.

Other prophets made the prediction appear still more convincing by coating the wall with smooth plaster.

But God's righteous judgment would come like a storm and destroy the poorly constructed wall when the Chaldeans devastated the land.

Hopes of peace and happiness that God's word does not authorize are deceptive.

They resemble a wall with a beautiful finish but no sound foundation.

False prophetesses mislead the people (verses 17–23)

It is a terrible thing to prefer pleasant lies to painful truths.

The false prophetesses tried to persuade the people that they were safe.

Henry understands their acts as imagery of giving people ease and encouraging pride through elaborate decorations.

Their schemes would fail, and God would free his people from their influence.

Christians must remain close to God's word and seek the Holy Spirit's teaching in everything.

Let us trust his promises in such a way that we also obey his commandments.

They were not praying prophets, had no intercourse with Heaven; they contrived how to please people, not how to do them good; they stood not against sin. They flattered people into vain hopes. Such widen the breach, by causing men to think themselves deserving of eternal life, when the wrath of God abides upon them.

Verses 10-16 One false prophet built the wall, set up the notion that Jerusalem should be victorious, and made himself acceptable by it. Others made the matter yet more plausible and promising; they daubed the wall which the first had built; but they would, ere long, be undeceived when their work was beaten down by the storm of God's just wrath; when the Chaldean army desolated the land. Verses 17-23 It is ill with those who had rather hear pleasing lies than unpleasing truths. Idols in the heart make outward worship empty (verses 1–11)

No outward religious ceremony or reform can be acceptable to God while an idol rules the heart.

Yet many people prefer their own inventions and supposed righteousness to God's appointed way of salvation.

Sinful desires and corrupt habits become idols people set up within themselves.

God may let them continue down that path.

Sin makes a person hateful in the sight of the pure and holy God.

It also becomes hateful to the sinner when conscience finally awakens.

Let us seek to be cleansed from both the guilt and the pollution of sin in the fountain God has opened.

Judgment and the limits of others' righteousness (verses 12–23)

National sins bring national judgments.

A sinner who escapes one judgment may still encounter another.

When people who publicly profess God's name rebel against him, they have reason to expect his judgment.

Noah's faith, obedience and prayer helped save his household, but did not save the whole world.

Job's offerings and prayers for his friends were accepted.

Daniel's intercession helped preserve his companions and the wise men of Babylon.

Yet a people who have reached the full measure of wickedness cannot expect to escape God's announced judgment simply because righteous people live among them.

Even the holiest believers are accepted personally only through Christ's suffering and righteousness.

Nevertheless, even amid the most widespread devastation, God preserves some people as living examples of his mercy.

We may trust that we will ultimately recognize the wisdom and justice of all his dealings, both with ourselves and with humanity.

Let this confidence quiet our rebellious murmuring and objections.

Verses 1-11 No outward form or reformation can be acceptable to God, so long as any idol possesses the heart; yet how many prefer their own devices and their own righteousness, to the way of salvation! Men's corruptions are idols in their hearts, and are of their own setting up; God will let them take their course. Sin renders the sinner odious in the eyes of the pure and holy God; and in his own eyes also, whenever conscience is awakened. Let us seek to be cleansed from the guilt and pollution of sins, in that fountain which the Lord has opened.
[Ezek.14.12-Ezek.14.23]
Verses 12-23 National sins bring national judgments. Though sinners escape one judgment, another is waiting for them. When God's professing people rebel against him, they may justly expect all his judgments. The faith, obedience, and prayers of Noah prevailed to the saving of his house, but not of the old world. Job's sacrifice and prayer in behalf of his friends were accepted, and Daniel had prevailed for the saving his companions and the wise men of Babylon. But a people that had filled the measure of their sins, was not to expect to escape for the sake of any righteous men living among them; not even of the most eminent saints, who could be accepted in their own case only through the sufferings and righteousness of Christ. Yet even when God makes the greatest desolations by his judgments, he saves some to be monuments of his mercy. In firm belief that we shall approve the whole of God's dealings with ourselves, and with all mankind, let us silence all rebellious murmurs and objections.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Jerusalem like an unfruitful vine.

Jerusalem as an unfruitful vine

A vine is valuable when it produces fruit.

If it bears none, its wood is nearly useless and is fit only to be thrown into the fire.

In the same way, human beings are capable of producing precious fruit by living for God.

This is the true purpose for which we exist.

If people refuse that purpose completely, their lives produce none of the fruit they were made to bear and end in ruin.

How blind are those who live in total neglect of God and genuine religion!

The picture applies especially to Jerusalem.

Let us beware of an outward profession of faith that bears no fruit.

Instead, let us come to Christ, remain in him, and seek to have his words remain in us.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.15.1]
Chapter 15
Jerusalem like an unfruitful vine.
If a vine be fruitful, it is valuable. But if not fruitful, it is worthless and useless, it is cast into the fire. Thus man is capable of yielding a precious fruit, in living to God; this is the sole end of his existence; and if he fails in this, he is of no use but to be destroyed. What blindness then attaches to those who live in the total neglect of God and of true religion! This similitude is applied to Jerusalem. Let us beware of an unfruitful profession. Let us come to Christ, and seek to abide in him, and to have his words abide in us.

modern_osis:
Original heading

A parable showing the first low estate of the Jewish nation, its prosperity, idolatries, and punishment.

Jerusalem's history pictured as an unfaithful woman (verses 1–58)

This chapter recounts God's dealings with the Jewish nation and the way the people responded to him.

It also describes the punishment that came through the surrounding nations—even through those in whom the Jews had trusted most.

The account is told as an extended parable.

An abandoned infant is rescued from death, brought up and cared for, joined in marriage and generously provided for.

Later, despite such kindness, she commits the most shameful acts of unfaithfulness and is punished for them.

Yet in the end she is received into favor and becomes ashamed of the conduct she had committed.

We must understand these expressions with regard to the customs, language and circumstances of their own time, rather than judging their tone entirely by modern expectations.

Many phrases that now seem shocking would have sounded different to their original hearers.

The purpose of the imagery was to inspire abhorrence of idolatry.

Henry believes this kind of parable was especially well suited to that end.

God remembers mercy and covenant (verses 59–63)

After a full warning of coming judgment, the Lord remembers mercy.

Mercy remains reserved for his people.

These closing verses contain a precious promise.

Part of it was fulfilled when repentant, reformed Jews returned from Babylon.

But Henry understands it to reach a fuller fulfillment in the gospel age.

God's gracious mercy should melt our hearts and awaken genuine sorrow over sin.

He will never leave a sinner to perish who humbles himself for sin and trusts in divine mercy and grace through Jesus Christ.

He will preserve that person by his power, through faith unto salvation.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.16.1-Ezek.16.58]
Chapter 16
A parable showing the first low estate of the Jewish nation, its prosperity, idolatries, and punishment.
Verses 1-58 In this chapter God's dealings with the Jewish nation, and their conduct towards him, are described, and their punishment through the surrounding nations, even those they most trusted in. This is done under the parable of an exposed infant rescued from death, educated, espoused, and richly provided for, but afterwards guilty of the most abandoned conduct, and punished for it; yet at last received into favour, and ashamed of her base conduct. We are not to judge of these expressions by modern ideas, but by those of the times and places in which they were used, where many of them would not sound as they do to us. The design was to raise hatred to idolatry, and such a parable was well suited for that purpose.
[Ezek.16.59-Ezek.16.63]
Verses 59-63 After a full warning of judgments, mercy is remembered, mercy is reserved. These closing verses are a precious promise, in part fulfilled at the return of the penitent and reformed Jews out of Babylon, but to have fuller accomplishment in gospel times. The Divine mercy should be powerful to melt our hearts into godly sorrow for sin. Nor will God ever leave the sinner to perish, who is humbled for his sins, and comes to trust in His mercy and grace through Jesus Christ; but will keep him by his power, through faith unto salvation.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesA parable relative to the Jewish nation.1–10to which an explanation is added.11–21A direct promise of the Messiah.22–24
The parable of the great eagles (verses 1–10)

Powerful conquerors are aptly compared with birds or beasts of prey.

Yet their destructive passions are directed and overruled to accomplish God's purposes.

Those who depart from the Lord and then seek security by changing from one earthly support to another merely change the form of their sin.

They will not truly prosper.

The parable is explained and Zedekiah rebuked (verses 11–21)

The prophecy now explains the parable through the history of the Jewish nation.

Zedekiah had been ungrateful to his benefactor, which was itself a sin against God.

In every solemn oath, the one who swears calls God as a witness to the truthfulness of the promise.

We owe truth to everyone, not only to members of our own religion.

When people who profess true religion betray those who practice false religion, their profession makes their wrongdoing more serious, not less.

God will punish their treachery even more severely.

He will not leave unpunished those who misuse his name.

No one who dies still bearing unrepented guilt will escape God's righteous judgment.

God promises the Messiah (verses 22–24)

Human unbelief cannot make God's promise fail.

The tree imagery used earlier as a threat now becomes part of a promise.

Henry understands this promise as referring especially to Jesus Christ, the Son of David, God's Messiah.

Satan's kingdom has long exercised great power, but it will be broken.

Christ's kingdom, once despised and disregarded, will be firmly established.

Blessed be God: our Redeemer will be known to the farthest ends of the earth.

Under his shadow we may find refuge from the coming wrath and from every spiritual enemy and danger.

Believers bear fruit in him.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesGod has no respect of persons.1–20The Divine providence is vindicated.21–29A gracious invitation to repentance.30–32
Everyone is responsible before God (verses 1–20)

“The soul that sins shall die.”

With respect to eternal life, people are treated according to their true standing: either under the old covenant of works or under the new covenant of grace, as their conduct shows.

People may suffer outwardly because of sins committed by others.

But we also have sins of our own, and God governs every circumstance for the eternal good of believers.

Every soul belongs to the great Creator.

He deals with all in justice or mercy.

No one is condemned eternally merely for another person's sin while remaining personally innocent of guilt.

All of us have sinned.

If God judged us only by his holy law, we would be lost.

Yet he invites us to come to Jesus Christ.

Consider the children of different parents.

A person whose faith is demonstrated by good works may have a wicked child whose character is entirely unlike that parent's.

The child cannot expect to escape judgment through the parent's godliness.

Likewise, a wicked person's child who walks righteously before God will not be destroyed for the sins of the parent.

That righteous child may still suffer in this life, but will share in salvation.

This chapter is not explaining how anyone earns justification.

It describes the Lord's righteous dealings with the wicked and the righteous.

God receives the person who turns from sin (verses 21–29)

A wicked person who turns from evil ways may be saved.

The person who truly repents truly believes.

Former sins are no longer held against that person.

The righteousness shown afterward is the fruit of faith and the result of conversion, not the purchase price of salvation.

The passage does not settle the separate question of whether a genuinely righteous believer can finally apostatize.

Many people who were thought righteous for a time later turn away from God.

But verses 26–27 display the fullness of his forgiving mercy.

When sin is forgiven, it is blotted out and remembered no more.

The believer lives in righteousness, not because that righteousness pays for former sins.

Holy living itself is a blessing purchased through the Mediator.

What encouragement this offers sinners returning to God!

Verse 28 describes both the beginning of repentance and how it continues.

Genuine believers remain watchful and prayerful and continue to the end, and thus are saved.

Whenever we dispute with God, he is right and we are wrong.

The Lord calls his people to repentance (verses 30–32)

The Lord will judge each Israelite according to that person's ways.

On this basis he calls them to repent and receive a new heart and new spirit.

God commands his people to take seriously the responsibilities within their reach and to pray for the inward change that only he can give.

He has appointed means of grace and ordinances and given both directions and promises.

Those who desire a new heart should therefore seek it from him.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.18.1-Ezek.18.20]
Chapter 18
God has no respect of persons. ( [Ezek.18.1-Ezek.18.20] Ezek 18:1-20) The Divine providence is vindicated. ( [Ezek.18.21-Ezek.18.29] Ezek 18:21-29) A gracious invitation to repentance. ( [Ezek.18.30-Ezek.18.32] Ezek 18:30-32)
Verses 1-20 The soul that sinneth it shall die. As to eternity, every man was, is, and will be dealt with, as his conduct shows him to have been under the old covenant of works, or the new covenant of grace. Whatever outward sufferings come upon men through the sins of others, they deserve for their own sins all they suffer; and the Lord overrules every event for the eternal good of believers. All souls are in the hand of the great Creator: he will deal with them in justice or mercy; nor will any perish for the sins of another, who is not in some sense worthy of death for his own. We all have sinned, and our souls must be lost, if God deal with us according to his holy law; but we are invited to come to Christ. If a man who had shown his faith by his works, had a wicked son, whose character and conduct were the reverse of his parent's, could it be expected he should escape the Divine vengeance on account of his father's piety? Surely not. And should a wicked man have a son who walked before God as righteous, this man would not perish for his father's sins. If the son was not free from evils in this life, still he should be partaker of salvation. The question here is not about the meritorious ground of justification, but about the Lord's dealings with the righteous and the wicked.
[Ezek.18.21-Ezek.18.29]
Verses 21-29 The wicked man would be saved, if he turned from his evil ways. The true penitent is a true believer. None of his former transgressions shall be mentioned unto him, but in the righteousness which he has done, as the fruit of faith and the effect of conversion, he shall surely live. The question is not whether the truly righteous ever become apostates. It is certain that many who for a time were thought to be righteous, do so, while [Ezek.18.26] Ezek 18:26, [Ezek.18.27] 27 speaks the fulness of pardoning mercy: when sin is forgiven, it is blotted out, it is remembered no more. In their righteousness they shall live; not for their righteousness, as if that were an atonement for their sins, but in their righteousness, which is one of the blessings purchased by the Mediator. What encouragement a repenting, returning sinner has to hope for pardon and life according to this promise! In verse 28 is the beginning and progress of repentance. True believers watch and pray, and continue to the end, and they are saved. In all our disputes with God, he is in the right, and we are in the wrong.
[Ezek.18.30-Ezek.18.32]
Verses 30-32 The Lord will judge each of the Israelites according to his ways. On this is grounded an exhortation to repent, and to make them a new heart and a new spirit. God does not command what cannot be done, but admonishes us to do what is in our power, and to pray for what is not. Ordinances and means are appointed, directions and promises are given, that those who desire this change may seek it from God.

Judah's kings are pictured as young lions (verses 1–9)

Ezekiel compares the kingdom of Judah to a lioness, and its kings to her young lions.

These rulers were cruel and oppressive toward their own people.

We should acknowledge God's righteousness when those who terrified and enslaved others are in turn terrified and enslaved.

When people who profess faith form close relationships with the ungodly, their children often grow up following the standards and fashions of a wicked world.

Receiving greater authority exposes the ambition and self-interest hidden in human hearts.

Those who devote their lives to harmful acts often bring them to an end through violence.

Jerusalem is pictured as a ruined vine (verses 10–14)

Jerusalem had once been like a fruitful, thriving vine.

Now the vine had been ruined, though its roots were not completely pulled up.

Through wickedness, the people had made themselves like dry tinder waiting for the sparks of God's judgment.

Even their own branches became fuel for their destruction.

Yet blessed be God!

One Branch belonging to the royal line pictured here not only became a strong rod fit for a ruler's scepter.

He is the true and living Vine himself.

All God's chosen people, through every generation, may rejoice in him.
classic_reading:
[Ezek.19.1-Ezek.19.9]
Chapter 19
A parable lamenting the ruin of Jehoahaz and Jehoiakim. ( [Ezek.19.1-Ezek.19.9] Ezek 19:1-9) Another describing the desolation of the people. ( [Ezek.19.10-Ezek.19.14] Ezek 19:10-14)
Verses 1-9 Ezekiel is to compare the kingdom of Judah to a lioness. He must compare the kings of Judah to a lion's whelps; they were cruel and oppressive to their own subjects. The righteousness of God is to be acknowledged, when those who have terrified and enslaved others, are themselves terrified and enslaved. When professors of religion form connexions with ungodly persons, their children usually grow up following after the maxims and fashions of a wicked world. Advancement to authority discovers the ambition and selfishness of men's hearts; and those who spend their lives in mischief, generally end them by violence.
[Ezek.19.10-Ezek.19.14]
Verses 10-14 Jerusalem was a vine, flourishing and fruitful. This vine is now destroyed, though not plucked up by the roots. She has by wickedness made herself like tinder to the sparks of God's wrath, so that her own branches serve as fuel to burn her. Blessed be God, one Branch of the vine here alluded to, is not only become a strong rod for the sceptre of those that rule, but is Himself the true and living Vine. This shall be for a rejoicing to all the chosen people of God throughout all generations.

The elders are reminded of Israel's sins in Egypt (verses 1–9)

People have become terribly hardened when they ask God to let them continue sinning, even while already suffering for sin.

See Ezekiel 20:32.

God is rightly angry with people who remain determined to persist in their wrongdoing.

Ezekiel was to remind the nation of its ancestors' evil deeds so that they would recognize the justice of God's earlier judgments.

The people rebelled in the wilderness (verses 10–26)

Israel's wilderness history is recalled in both the Old Testament and the New Testament as a warning.

God had done wonderful things for his people.

He gave them his law and renewed the ancient observance of the Sabbath.

Sabbaths are privileges and signs of belonging to him.

When we honor their purpose, we discover that God himself makes us holy and truly happy in this life, preparing us for the perfect holiness and happiness of heaven.

But the Israelites rebelled and were left to suffer the judgments their sins had brought.

Sometimes God permits sin to become its own punishment.

Yet God is never the author of sin.

People may be made thoroughly miserable simply by being handed over to their own evil desires and passions.

Israel's rebellion continued in Canaan (verses 27–32)

After the people settled in Canaan, they continued rebelling.

The elders listening to Ezekiel seemed to be considering merging with the surrounding nations and their worship.

An outward profession of faith accomplishes nothing if it remains only a profession.

Sinful compromise brings no real advantage.

The worldly schemes of hypocrites will ultimately be useless to them.

God promises to restore and renew a remnant (verses 33–44)

Wicked Israelites who followed other nations in sin would not share those nations' prosperity.

Instead, God would separate them for judgment.

No one can escape the Lord's rule.

Those who refuse to submit to the power of his grace will face the power of his wrath.

But God will not lose a single one of his jewels amid the confusion of the world.

He will bring the Jews back to Israel's land and give them genuine repentance.

Their hearts will be overcome by his kindness.

The more we know of God's holiness, the more clearly we recognize how hateful sin is.

People who remain unmoved despite God's gracious means, and who insist on living without Christ like the surrounding world, are moving toward destruction.

Judgment is announced against fruitless Jerusalem (verses 45–49)

Judah and Jerusalem had been full of people, like a forest filled with trees.

Yet they produced no good fruit.

God's word speaks against those who refuse to bear the fruits of righteousness.

When he determines to bring a nation low, who can rescue it?

Even the clearest truths sounded like parables to the people.

Those who refuse to respond to God's word commonly blame the message rather than admit their unwillingness to obey.

Chapter 20
The elders of Israel are reminded of the idolatry in Egypt. ( [Ezek.20.1-Ezek.20.9] Ezek 20:1-9) In the wilderness. ( [Ezek.20.10-Ezek.20.26] Ezek 20:10-26) In Canaan. ( [Ezek.20.27-Ezek.20.32] Ezek 20:27-32) God promises to pardon and restore them. ( [Ezek.20.33-Ezek.20.44] Ezek 20:33-44) Prophecy against Jerusalem. ( [Ezek.20.45-Ezek.20.49] Ezek 20:45-49)
Verses 1-9 . Those hearts are wretchedly hardened which ask God leave to go on in sin, and that even when suffering for it; see [Ezek.20.32] Ezek 20:32. God is justly angry with those who are resolved to go on still in their trespasses. Cause the people to know the evil deeds of their fathers, that they may see how righteous it was with God to cut them off.
[Ezek.20.10-Ezek.20.26]
Verses 10-26 . The history of Israel in the wilderness is referred to in the new Testament as well as in the Old, for warning. God did great things for them. He gave them the law, and revived the ancient keeping of the sabbath day. Sabbaths are privileges; they are signs of our being his people. If we do the duty of the day, we shall find, to our comfort, it is the Lord that makes us holy, that is, truly happy, here; and prepares us to be happy, that is, perfectly holy, hereafter. The Israelites rebelled, and were left to the judgments they brought upon themselves. God sometimes makes sin to be its own punishment, yet he is not the Author of sin: there needs no more to make men miserable, than to give them up to their own evil desires and passions.
[Ezek.20.27-Ezek.20.32]
Verses 27-32 The Jews persisted in rebellion after they settled in the land of Canaan. And these elders seem to have thought of uniting with the heathen. We make nothing by our profession if it be but a profession. There is nothing got by sinful compliances; and the carnal projects of hypocrites will stand them in no stead.
[Ezek.20.33-Ezek.20.44]
Verses 33-44 The wicked Israelites, notwithstanding they follow the sinful ways of other nations, shall not mingle with them in their prosperity, but shall be separated from them for destruction. There is no shaking off God's dominion; and those who will not yield to the power of his grace, shall sink under the power of his wrath. But not one of God's jewels shall be lost in the lumber of this world. He will bring the jews to the land of Israel again; and will give them true repentance. They will be overcome with his kindness: the more we know of God's holiness, the more we see the hateful nature of sin. Those who remain unaffected amidst means of grace, and would live without Christ, like the world around them, may be sure it is the way to destruction.
[Ezek.20.45-Ezek.20.49]
Verses 45-49 Judah and Jerusalem had been full of people, as a forest of trees, but empty of fruit. God's word prophesies against those who bring not forth the fruits of righteousness. When He will ruin a nation, who or what can save it? The plainest truths were as parables to the people. It is common for those who will not be wrought upon by the word, to blame it.
